question: This is a customer-service call in contemporary Spanish as spoken in Madrid, Spain. Does this utterance use natural Madrid Spanish without translationese or unnatural word choice, and with correct verb forms and basic function words?
native_does: Natural conversational Madrid Spanish appropriate to a customer-service call passes, including ordinary formal or informal speech and established English borrowings or code-switching when they sound natural in context. Literal names, identifiers, and genuinely user-visible product, interface, setting, or status labels that must be preserved may remain in English when naturally integrated. Vocabulary and grammar must be natural in contemporary Madrid Spanish, with an internally consistent regional variety; regional validity elsewhere does not by itself pass. Judge language use only, not factual or task correctness.
ai_likely_does: Inspect every complete clause independently. Permitted English, technical material, or natural wording elsewhere does not excuse a separate defect. Flag language that would sound clearly odd, ungrammatical, or non-Madrid in this setting, including English-shaped or word-for-word service phrasing or result constructions; unnatural word choice, collocation, or customer-facing backend language; avoidable raw English where Spanish is ordinarily expected; a clear error in verb form, subject-verb person or number, required clitics or governed prepositions, ser/estar, por/para, or other basic function words; and lexical, grammatical, or second-person forms that are not natural in contemporary Madrid Spanish. Also flag within-utterance mixing of Madrid and non-Madrid regional varieties. One clear marker in the utterance is sufficient; it need not recur across the call. Also flag missing, extra, or misplaced written Spanish diacritics, including accent marks, ñ, and ü, when standard orthography requires them. Ignore only a diacritic issue that is part of an obvious transcription artifact or the clipped ending of an interrupted turn. Quotation marks or apparent system provenance alone do not make an untranslated generic category or ordinary service term acceptable. Also flag a generic customer-data word when its ordinary Spanish meaning does not naturally identify the specific field being requested. A merely smoother, more specialized, or more formal alternative is not enough. Do not flag gender agreement, politeness, or mere switching between otherwise natural Madrid formal and informal forms of address. For interrupted turns, judge complete material before the cutoff and ignore only the clipped ending.
